one_liner: Vulkan GPU builder for PHOBIC minimal perfect hash functions; builds about 62x faster than 8-thread CPU PHOBIC.
what_it_does: Builds a minimal perfect hash function (a bijection from n keys to [0, n)) for a std::vector of std::string, uint64_t, std::pair<uint64_t,uint64_t> or pre-hashed 128-bit Key. Bucket assignment, bucket sorting and the seed search run on the GPU, and the result is an ordinary CPU-side object queried with f(key). You use it as `MPHFbuilder b(MPHFconfig(lambda, partitionSize)); MPHF<PilotEncoder, OffsetEncoder, xxhash> f; b.build(keys, f); f(key)`. The typedefs FastQueryMphf (interleaved Compact) and SmallSpaceMphf (interleaved Rice) cover the common cases. It uses its own phobicgpu:: types, so it cannot be swapped in for pthash's PHOBIC classes.
how_it_is_fast: It runs the PHOBIC algorithm: PTHash-style bucket placement with an optimized bucket-size distribution (OptBucketer), tiny partitions of about 2,048-2,500 keys, and interleaved coding of the seeds. Each partition maps to one Vulkan compute workgroup, and that partition's occupancy bitmap fits in fast shared memory. A per-partition counting-sort shader orders buckets by decreasing size. All threads in the workgroup then search seeds together with a single-loop version of the usual seed/key nested loop: a shared atomicAdd hands out the next candidate, and atomicMin keeps the smallest working seed, which avoids warp divergence. Seeds encode p = s*m + d (an additive displacement), so trying the next candidate only adds 1 to cached positions. The CPU uses OpenMP for the xxHash3-128 master hashing and the final Rice/Compact encoding.
when_to_use: Rebuilding large MPHFs (the paper benchmarks 10^8 string keys) where build time dominates and a desktop GPU is idle: 27-28 ns/key vs 1,781 ns/key for 8-thread CPU PHOBIC at lambda=9.

Space-efficient settings (lambda 9-14, about 1.67-1.76 bits/key) that are too slow to build on a CPU. For example, lambda=13 gives 1.68 bits/key at 560 ns/key on the GPU, and the paper says much larger lambda is not feasible on the CPU.
Query-heavy lookup tables that need PTHash-class CPU query latency (37-52 ns) but GPU-speed builds. RecSplit-GPU builds equally fast but queries in 126-147 ns.
Linux machines with a Vulkan 1.3 GPU that supports VK_KHR_maintenance4, where build energy matters: the paper measures about 30x less energy per build than the 8-thread CPU.
when_not_to_use: Small inputs or small lambda. Moving the keys to the GPU dominates there: Fig. 6 in the paper shows the GPU needs large n (many partitions) and large lambda to pay off.
When you need faster queries. Queries run the same CPU code as PHOBIC, so only construction gets faster.

When you need to save and load the function, build in external memory, or go past 2^32 keys. The MPHF class has no serialization, the key count is a uint32_t, and all keys are uploaded to the device at once (16 bytes/key for the key buffer alone). pthash covers these cases.
Machines without a Vulkan GPU and driver. Only an Nvidia RTX 3090 on Linux was benchmarked, and CI only builds on Ubuntu 22.04 without running anything.
Production use without in-house maintenance: this is research code with 4 stars, one merged PR, no issues filed, and GPL-3.0 copyleft.

integration.dependencies: Vulkan SDK (libvulkan, headers, glslc shader compiler), OpenMP; git submodules xxHash, jermp/essentials, tlx (benchmark CLI only); bundled fastmod.h
integration.min_toolchain: C++17, CMake 3.19+, Vulkan 1.3 (shaders compiled with --target-env=vulkan1.3, SPIR-V 1.5); the paper used GCC 11.4.0
integration.platforms: Linux with a Vulkan 1.3 GPU that has VK_KHR_maintenance4 (prefers a discrete GPU; benchmarked only on an Nvidia RTX 3090); the query-side code is plain C++
integration.thread_safety: Not documented. The builder shares a process-wide Vulkan singleton (App::getInstance()) and one compute queue, so assume one build at a time. Queries use a const, read-only operator().
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial — same algorithm with nearly the same space and query time as CPU PHOBIC (1.76 vs 1.74 bits/key, 52 vs 50 ns at lambda=9), but it is a separate phobicgpu::MPHF type with its own encoders and no save/load, so it is not interchangeable with pthash::phobic / dense_partitioned_phf

gotchas: Compiled shaders are loaded at runtime from the relative path "shaders/<name>.comp.spv" under the current working directory, but the build writes them to ${CMAKE_BINARY_DIR}/shaders. A process started from any other directory throws "failed to open file".
The README says to link `PHOBIC-GPU`, but the CMake target is actually `GpuPTHash` (MPHF-Experiments links `GpuPTHash`).

Debug builds (NDEBUG unset) turn on VK_LAYER_KHRONOS_validation and throw std::runtime_error if the layer is not installed. All Vulkan failures, including out-of-memory on the device, are reported as std::runtime_error.

The example says the partition size should be tuned for your GPU (defaults: 2,048 in MPHFconfig, 2,500 in the paper). MPHF-Experiments has to `#undef MAX_BUCKET_SIZE` between including pthash.hpp and phobic_gpu_mphf.hpp.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Choose this over PTHash, whose master branch now ships CPU PHOBIC as pthash::phobic, only when you have a Vulkan GPU and build time on about 10^8 keys dominates; PTHash gives the same query path plus serialization and multithreaded or external-memory builds. Choose it over GpuRecSplit (CUDA) when query latency matters: build speed is similar (27 vs 24 ns/key at about 1.8 bits/key) but CPU queries take 52 ns vs 126 ns; GpuRecSplit is the better choice below 1.6 bits/key (1.58 bits/key at 80 ns/key).
verified_claims_summary: The authors' PHOBIC paper (arXiv 2404.18497, ESA 2024, Table 1) built MPHFs on 100M random 10-50 character strings. PHOBIC-GPU (RTX 3090 via Vulkan 1.3.236, plus 8 CPU threads) took 27 ns/key at lambda=9 with interleaved Rice coding (1.76 bits/key, 52 ns CPU query). The authors' own CPU PHOBIC took 1,781 ns/key with 8 threads and 9,171 ns/key with 1 thread on an i7-11700 (GCC 11.4.0 -O3 -march=native). The text calls this a 62x speedup (the table itself gives about 66x) and about 30x less energy (405 W vs 195 W draw). No std:: baseline is involved: this compares the same algorithm on a GPU and on a CPU.
status_note: Stale research code: the last commit (2025-07-03) only edited the README, and the last code change was 2025-03-20. It has 4 stars and is GPL-3.0 (but CITATION.cff says AGPL-3.0-or-later). You can use it via CMake add_subdirectory, but expect to fix things yourself.
